The wind on the Isle of Skerry didn’t just blow; it screamed. It tore at the stone walls of the lighthouse, a constant, rhythmic assault that Elias had endured for thirty years. He was old now, his joints stiff as rusted hinges, and his eyes, once sharp enough to spot a gull from a mile out, were clouded by cataracts. The light above him still turned, a mechanical heartbeat in the dark, but Elias felt he was fading into the same obscurity as the rocks below.

On a Tuesday, when the storm was at its peak, the mail boat arrived. It was an anomaly. The sea was too rough for the small skiff to navigate the channel safely. Yet there it was, bobbing violently against the jetty, carrying a single, wax-sealed envelope.

Elias pulled it aboard with trembling hands. The paper was thick, cream-colored, and smelled faintly of ozone and rain—scents that did not belong to this damp, salt-heavy world. There was no return address, only his name written in a script that looked like it had been printed by a machine rather than penned by a hand.

*Dear Elias,*

*You are wondering how I know your name. You are wondering if this is a trick of the mind, brought on by isolation and age. It is neither. I am you, forty years hence. Or perhaps, I am what you could have been.*

Elias’s breath hitched. He sat on the cold floorboards, the letter clutched to his chest. The lighthouse beam swept across the room, painting the walls in stark white and black.

*Do not fix the lens mechanism tomorrow,* the letter continued. *When the gear slips, do not attempt to force it back into place. Let it slip. The light will dim for three nights. The ships will complain. The authorities will send inspectors. They will reprimand you. But they will also replace the entire optical assembly with a new model, one that burns brighter and reaches further. If you fix it, the old glass remains. And in 1924, the *Hesperus* will miss the turn because the light wasn't bright enough to cut through the fog. If you let it fail, the *Hesperus* turns safe. Forty-two lives are saved.*

Elias stared at the words. The *Hesperus*. He remembered the ship. It had passed the island twenty years
